hints: Work out each chloride formula from the oxidation state of the Period 3 element, Na is +1, Mg is +2, Si is +4, with chloride as $\text{Cl}^-$.
Decide giant or simple by position in Period 3, metals on the left form giant ionic lattices while Si forms discrete covalent molecules.
Recall what happens in water, ionic NaCl just dissolves neutrally, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ slightly hydrolyses, and $\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolyses fully to give $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Get the formulae from charges**
Think of each metal losing electrons to form $\text{Cl}^-$. Sodium forms $\text{Na}^+$, so you need one $\text{Cl}^-$ to give $\text{NaCl}$. Magnesium forms $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, so you need two $\text{Cl}^-$ to give $\text{MgCl}_2$. Silicon is in Group 14 with oxidation state +4 in its chloride, so you need four $\text{Cl}^-$ to give $\text{SiCl}_4$.

Link position to structure and bonding**
Na and Mg are metals, so their chlorides are giant ionic lattices with strong ionic bonding between oppositely charged ions. Silicon is a metalloid forming a covalent chloride, so $\text{SiCl}_4$ exists as discrete simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, with strong covalent bonds inside each molecule.

Predict the pH behaviour in water**
$\text{NaCl}$ just dissociates into hydrated ions with no hydrolysis, so the solution stays neutral at pH 7. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small and highly charging so it weakly hydrolyses to release a little $\text{H}^+$, giving the slightly acidic pH 6.2. $\text{SiCl}_4$ reacts fully with water: $\text{SiCl}_4 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Si(OH)}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$, so strong acid $\text{HCl}$ makes pH very low, about 1 to 2.

Final answer: Formula: $\text{NaCl}$ ; $\text{MgCl}_2$ ; $\text{SiCl}_4$
Structure and bonding: $\text{NaCl}$ giant ionic ; $\text{MgCl}_2$ giant ionic ; $\text{SiCl}_4$ simple covalent
pH: $\text{NaCl}$ pH 7 ; $\text{MgCl}_2$ pH 6.2 (given) ; $\text{SiCl}_4$ pH 1 to 4, strongly acidic.

hints: Focus on the clue that the same $\text{Cl}_2$ is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction.
walkthrough:
Recognise simultaneous oxidation and reduction of one species**
Here $\text{Cl}_2$ with oxidation state 0 goes to $\text{Cl}^-$ in $\text{NaCl}$ where Cl is -1 (reduction) and also to Cl in +1 in G (oxidation). When the same element is both oxidised and reduced at the same time, the special name is disproportionation.
Final answer: Disproportionation

hints: Recall the familiar bleach reaction where cold dilute $\text{NaOH}$ oxidises $\text{Cl}_2$ only to oxidation state +1.
walkthrough:
Recall the cold alkali product**
With cold $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, the equation is $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Chlorine goes from 0 to -1 and 0 to +1. The +1 product is $\text{ClO}^-$, so G is $\text{NaClO}$.
Final answer: $\text{NaClO}$, sodium chlorate(I) / sodium hypochlorite

hints: Remember hot concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ pushes oxidation further to Cl in oxidation state +5 as $\text{ClO}_3^-$.
walkthrough:
Write the hot alkali disproportionation**
Hot conditions give the chlorate(V), $\text{ClO}_3^-$, where Cl is +5, alongside chloride where Cl is -1. Balancing Cl, Na, O and H gives $$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaClO}_3 + 5\text{NaCl} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms balance on both sides.

hints: Recall the colour of the silver halide precipitate formed when $\text{Ag}^+$ meets $\text{Cl}^-$.
Recall how $\text{AgCl}$ behaves differently from $\text{AgBr}$ and $\text{AgI}$ when dilute $\text{NH}_3\text{(aq)}$ is added.
walkthrough:
Spot the white precipitate**
$\text{NaCl(aq)}$ provides $\text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})$. With $\text{AgNO}_3(\text{aq})$: $\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s)}$. This is seen as a white precipitate.

Test solubility in dilute ammonia**
$\text{AgCl}$ is the one silver halide that dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3\text{(aq)}$ to form the complex $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$, giving a colourless solution. This confirms chloride.

Final answer: White precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ forms.
Precipitate dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3\text{(aq)}$ to give a colourless solution.

hints: Count bonding pairs around P, $\text{PCl}_5$ has 5 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, $\text{PCl}_6^-$ has 6 bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
Recall the VSEPR shapes for 5 and 6 electron pairs with no lone pairs on the central atom.
walkthrough:
Apply VSEPR counting**
In $\text{PCl}_5$, phosphorus has 5 $\text{P-Cl}$ bonding pairs and zero lone pairs. Five pairs arrange to minimise repulsion as trigonal bipyramidal.

Extend to the six coordinate ion**
In $\text{PCl}_6^-$, phosphorus has 6 bonding pairs and zero lone pairs. Six pairs point to the corners of an octahedron, so the shape is octahedral. This fits with $\text{PCl}_4^+$ having 4 pairs and being tetrahedral.

Final answer: $\text{PCl}_5$: trigonal bipyramidal
$\text{PCl}_6^-$: octahedral ($\text{PCl}_4^+$ given as tetrahedral)

hints: Think what small molecule must supply O and H to turn $\text{PCl}_5$ into $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ plus $\text{HCl}$.
Name the reaction type where a chloride reacts with water to give an acid and $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Identify J as water**
To get $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ from $\text{PCl}_5$ you need oxygen and extra hydrogen. Water provides both: $\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$.

Name the reaction type**
Breaking down a covalent chloride using water to form an acid is classic hydrolysis. $\text{PCl}_5$ fumes in moist air for this reason.

Final answer: J is $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ / water
Type of reaction: hydrolysis

hints: Start by thinking how the electron rich $\text{C=C}$ repels electrons in $\text{Cl}_2$ to create a $\delta+$ and $\delta-$ end.
Recall the two step electrophilic addition route, attack by the alkene to form a carbocation, then attack by $\text{Cl}^-$ on the positive carbon.
Remember curly arrows show electron pair movement, from the double bond to $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$ and from the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond to $\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$.
Consider which carbocation is more stable to draw the correct intermediate from propene, the secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ or equivalent.
walkthrough:
Polarise the chlorine molecule**
As $\text{Cl}_2$ approaches the high electron density of the $\text{C=C}$ in propene, electrons are repelled to the far end. Label it $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$. The $\delta+$ end acts as the electrophile.

First curly arrow pair to make the carbocation**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=C}$ bond to the $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond onto the $\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$ to give $\text{Cl}^-$. This forms the more stable secondary carbocation, with Cl attached to one carbon and $\text{C}^+$ on the middle carbon.

Second step, capture by chloride**
Now the $\text{Cl}^-$ ion has lone pairs and the carbocation has an empty p orbital. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Cl}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$ centre. This forms the second $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and gives 1,2-dichloropropane.

Check charges and arrows**
Make sure dipoles, + charge on the intermediate carbon, - charge on chloride, and all curly arrows start at an electron pair and point to where the pair goes. That precision earns the mechanism marks.

Final answer: Electrophilic addition: $\text{Cl}_2$ polarised as $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{Cl}^{\delta+}$; curly arrow from $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond to $\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$ forming $\text{Cl}^-$ and carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (secondary); curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_2\text{Cl}$.

hints: Look at K to L, a $\text{HCl}$ molecule is lost from a chloroalkane to form a $\text{C=C}$, decide if this is substitution or elimination and which solvent favours it.
walkthrough:
Choose elimination conditions**
K is a dichloroalkane and L is a chloroalkene, so one $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated to create the double bond. Elimination of $\text{HX}$ needs hot ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$, not aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ which would give substitution to an alcohol.
Final answer: $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol, heat

hints: Open the $\text{C=C}$ of L, $\text{CCl(CH}_3\text{)=CH}_2$, to make a single $\text{C-C}$ link with continuation bonds and keep the Cl and $\text{CH}_3$ on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
Draw the repeat unit**
Addition polymerisation opens the double bond in L, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)CCl=CH}_2$, to single bonds. Join many monomers head to tail to give $$-[\text{CCl(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2]-$$ Show two continuation bonds extending from the two backbone carbons, with $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH}_3$ on one carbon and two H on the other.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{CCl(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2-$ with continuation bonds through the backbone, i.e. $-[\text{CCl(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2]-_n$
